About this citation

The corpus cites the same work under the German and the English form of its title. It is a two-volume collection of essays and aphorisms, and 'Aphorisms on the Wisdom of Life' is a section within the first volume rather than a separate work.

### Exact wording

English (as recorded here)

“Everyone takes the limits of his own field of vision for the limits of the world.”

German

“Jeder hält die Grenze seines Gesichtskreises für die Grenze der Welt.”

From Parerga und Paralipomena. English “field of vision” renders Gesichtskreis; some versions say “horizon.”

#### Forms in circulation that differ

-   “Everyone takes the limits of his own field of vision for the limits of the world.”
-   “Every man takes the limits of his own field of vision for the limits of the world.”

### Attribution notes

Schopenhauer, Parerga and Paralipomena (usually cited from the “Psychological Observations” / related aphoristic sections). It is not from The World as Will and Representation; sites that cite WWR are recycling a wrong default title for Schopenhauer.

#### About Arthur Schopenhauer

Arthur Schopenhauer (1788–1860) was a German philosopher of pessimism whose The World as Will and Representation fused Kantian phenomena with a blind metaphysical will. Largely ignored while Hegel dominated Berlin, he later won fame influencing artists and psychologists.

### Interpretation

Schopenhauer is diagnosing a specific error: mistaking the limits of one's own experience for the limits of what exists. The mechanism is that we cannot see outside our own field of vision, and the absence of anything visible is easily read as an absence of anything. He applies it to disagreements about what is possible, where each party treats their own horizon as the boundary of the world. The remark is aimed at complacency about the range of one's own experience.

#### Why it matters

It is a good check on confident claims about what cannot be done. The question it raises is whether the limit is in the thing or in what you can see from where you stand.

### Questions readers arrive with

#### What is the source of the quotation “Everyone takes the limits of his own field…”?

“Everyone takes the limits of his own field…” comes from Parerga und Paralipomena (1851), attributed to Arthur Schopenhauer.

#### What does Arthur Schopenhauer mean by knowledge?

Epistemology asks whether knowledge is justified true belief, reliable tracking of the world, or something else; it also asks how perception, testimony, memory, and reason contribute. This passage enters that discussion through knowledge.

#### Is the wording of this Arthur Schopenhauer quotation commonly changed?

The wording recorded here is “Everyone takes the limits of his own field of vision for the limits of the world.” Forms in circulation that differ: Everyone takes the limits of his own field of vision for the limits of the world. / Every man takes the limits of his own field of vision for the limits of the world. The German reads “Jeder hält die Grenze seines Gesichtskreises für die Grenze der Welt.”

#### Is this quotation attributed correctly?

Schopenhauer, Parerga and Paralipomena (usually cited from the “Psychological Observations” / related aphoristic sections). It is not from The World as Will and Representation; sites that cite WWR are recycling a wrong default title for Schopenhauer.
